coverage: Both full English editions, episodes 1-12 of 18. Named persons, and the writers, saints, heresiarchs and stage figures the characters quote. Peoples, places, newspapers, songs, pubs and shops are not cast.

entities.name: Stephen Dedalus
entities.body: The young man who wakes in the Martello tower at Sandycove: a poet and a teacher, in mourning for his mother and unwilling to say why he would not kneel at her deathbed. He pays the rent of the tower and carries its key. Mulligan calls him Kinch; the older edition and the modern edition agree on every form of his name.

entities.name: Buck Mulligan
entities.body: Malachi Mulligan, a medical student, who shares the tower with Stephen and opens the book shaving on its roof with a mock mass. He is Stephen’s friend and his tormentor in the same breath: he mimics him, borrows from him, and told his own mother that it was only Dedalus whose mother was beastly dead.

entities.name: Haines
entities.body: The Englishman staying in the tower, down from Oxford, collecting Irish folk sayings for a book. He raved all night about shooting a black panther, apologises for it in the morning, pays the milkwoman, and tells Stephen that England has treated Ireland rather unfairly and that history is to blame.

entities.name: Stephen’s mother
entities.body: Dead a year, and the presence the episode turns on. Stephen would not kneel and pray at her bedside when she asked him, and she comes to him in a dream in her loose brown graveclothes smelling of wax and rosewood. Mulligan says the aunt thinks Stephen killed her. She is not named in this episode.

entities.name: The milkwoman
entities.body: The old woman who brings the morning milk up to the tower, is spoken to in Irish by Haines and cannot understand it, and is paid a florin against a bill of two and two. Stephen sees in her the silk of the kine and the poor old woman, names given Ireland in old times: a wandering crone serving her conqueror and her gay betrayer.

entities.name: The young man in the water
entities.body: Clinging to a spur of rock at the fortyfoot hole, who brings Mulligan the news that Seymour has chucked medicine for the army and was spooning with the Carlisle girl on the pier.

entities.name: The elderly swimmer
entities.body: Who shoots up near the spur of rock with a blowing red face and scrambles past Mulligan out of the water.

entities.name: The boatman
entities.body: One of two men watching from the verge of the cliff, who says there are five fathoms out there and that the drowned man will be swept up when the tide comes in about one. It is nine days today.

entities.name: The businessman
entities.body: The other of the two.

entities.name: The drowned man
entities.body: Nine days in the bay, and the body the sail is waiting for. Stephen thinks of the swollen bundle bobbing up and rolling over a puffy saltwhite face to the sun, and of Mulligan, who has saved men from drowning as he has not.

entities.name: Mulligan’s aunt
entities.body: Who thinks Stephen killed his mother and will not let her nephew have anything to do with him, keeps plainlooking servants for Malachi, and might be got to fork out twenty quid for Athens.

entities.name: Ursula
entities.body: The aunt’s servant, out of whose room Mulligan pinched the cracked shaving mirror. Her name is the last word of the joke about keeping plainlooking servants.

entities.name: Mulligan’s mother
entities.body: Who came out of the drawingroom with a visitor and asked her son who was in his room, and got the answer Stephen has not forgiven: O, it’s only Dedalus whose mother is beastly dead.

entities.name: Mulligan’s brother
entities.body: Down in Westmeath with the Bannons.

entities.name: Cranly
entities.body: Whose arm Stephen remembers when Mulligan links his own in it. A friend of an earlier time, named only in that one thought.

entities.name: Seymour
entities.body: Who has chucked medicine and is going in for the army, and whom Mulligan would bring down to rag Haines if he made any noise in the tower. He was spooning with the Carlisle girl on the pier last night.

entities.name: Lily
entities.body: The red Carlisle girl, whose father is rotto with money.

entities.name: Bannon
entities.body: Who sent a card from Westmeath saying he had found a sweet young thing down there — a photo girl, he calls her.

entities.name: The Bannons
entities.body: The family in Westmeath that Mulligan’s brother is staying with.

entities.name: Clive Kempthorpe
entities.body: In whose Oxford rooms the moneyed voices shouted while he hopped round the table with his trousers at his heels and his shirt in ribbons, chased with a tailor’s shears — the ragging Mulligan offers to repeat on Haines.

entities.name: Aubrey
entities.body: One of the palefaces in that room, called on to break the news gently.

entities.name: Ades of Magdalen
entities.body: Who chased him with the tailor’s shears.

entities.name: Connolly Norman
entities.body: At Dottyville, where the fellow Mulligan was with in the Ship is a patient: general paralysis of the insane, which is what the fellow says Stephen has.

entities.name: Matthew Arnold
entities.body: Whose face masks the deaf gardener pushing a mower on the sombre Oxford lawn in Stephen’s vision of the quadrangle.

entities.name: Mother Grogan
entities.body: Who said that when she makes tea she makes tea and when she makes water she makes water — Mulligan’s piece of folk for Haines’s book, delivered in an old woman’s wheedling voice.

entities.name: Mrs Cahill
entities.body: To whom she said it, and who answered: God send you don’t make them in the one pot.

entities.name: Mary Ann
entities.body: Of the song Mulligan growls at the loaf, and whom Stephen guesses was a kinswoman of mother Grogan’s.

entities.name: Royce
entities.body: Old Royce, who sang in the pantomime of Turko the Terrible, and whom Stephen’s mother heard and laughed at with the others when she was a girl.

entities.name: Turko the Terrible
entities.body: The pantomime, and the boy of its song that can enjoy invisibility. Both editions keep the spelling.

entities.name: Swinburne
entities.body: Whom Mulligan asks whether the sea is not what he calls it: a great sweet mother. The older edition gives only the nickname Mulligan uses for him, Algy; the modern edition prints the surname instead.

entities.name: Oscar Wilde
entities.body: Whose Caliban Mulligan quotes at the cracked mirror, and whom he says the age has grown out of along with paradoxes.

entities.name: Caliban
entities.body: Whose rage at not seeing his face in a mirror Mulligan offers Stephen as the joke of the cracked lookingglass.

entities.name: Shakespeare
entities.body: Whose grandfather, Mulligan says, Stephen proves by algebra to be Hamlet’s grandson — and who is himself the ghost of his own father.

entities.name: Hamlet
entities.body: The play Haines asks Stephen for his idea of, and whose Elsinore the tower and cliffs remind him of.

entities.name: Thomas Aquinas
entities.body: And the fiftyfive reasons he has made out to prop the theory up, which Mulligan says he is not equal to before a few pints. Stephen calls him Aquinas tunbelly on the strand, frate porcospino, and quotes his morose delectation.

entities.name: Loyola
entities.body: Whom Mulligan tells Stephen to chuck and come down: the Sassenach wants his morning rashers.

entities.name: Fergus
entities.body: Who rules the brazen cars in the song Mulligan drones down the staircase, and which Stephen sang alone in the house at his mother’s open door.

entities.name: William Pitt
entities.body: Who had the Martello towers built, Mulligan says, when the French were on the sea. The older edition calls him Billy.

entities.name: Sir Peter Teazle
entities.body: Whom Stephen’s mother called the doctor in her last illness, while she picked buttercups off the quilt.

entities.name: Japhet
entities.body: In search of a father — what Mulligan calls Stephen in the ear, hearing his theory of Hamlet.

entities.name: Mercury
entities.body: Whose hat quivers on Mulligan’s head as he capers down to the fortyfoot hole, fluttering his winglike hands. The modern edition writes only “his hat”, so the god stands in the older edition alone.

entities.name: Chrysostomos
entities.body: The golden-mouthed: the one word Stephen thinks at the gold points glistening in Mulligan’s teeth. The modern edition drops the word altogether, so he stands in the older edition alone.

entities.name: Joseph the Joiner
entities.body: With whom the queerest young fellow of Mulligan’s ballad cannot agree. He walks the procession of saints in episode 12 as S. Joseph, between S. Alfred and S. Denis.

entities.name: Butterly
entities.body: The name at the end of Mulligan’s pun on the gospel: and going forth he met Butterly.

entities.name: Zarathustra
entities.body: Thus spake whom, Mulligan says solemnly, taking Stephen’s twopence: he who stealeth from the poor lendeth to the Lord.

entities.name: Pope Marcellus
entities.body: In whose mass the symbol of the apostles is sung, the voices blended, loud in affirmation — the music behind Stephen’s memory of the church militant and her heresiarchs.

entities.name: Photius
entities.body: First of the heresiarchs the vigilant angel menaces in Stephen’s memory, and of whose brood of mockers Mulligan is one.

entities.name: Arius
entities.body: Who warred his life long upon the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father.

entities.name: Valentine
entities.body: Who spurned Christ’s terrene body.

entities.name: Sabellius
entities.body: The African, subtlest heresiarch of them all, who held that the Father was Himself His own Son.

entities.name: Mr Garrett Deasy
entities.body: The headmaster of the school at Dalkey where Stephen teaches: an Ulster protestant and a unionist who pays Stephen his salary in sovereigns and shillings, lectures him on saving money, dictates a letter to the press about foot and mouth disease, and tells him that England is in the hands of the jews and that Ireland never persecuted them because she never let them in.

entities.name: Cochrane
entities.body: One of Stephen’s pupils, who is asked what city sent for Pyrrhus and answers Tarentum, and who is on the same side as Halliday at hockey.

entities.name: Armstrong
entities.body: The boy with the bag of figrolls in his satchel, asked what was the end of Pyrrhus and offering a pier. Welloff people, proud that their eldest son was in the navy; Vico Road, Dalkey.

entities.name: Comyn
entities.body: The boy who laughs, and who is told to ask Stephen about Pyrrhus.

entities.name: Talbot
entities.body: The boy who reads Lycidas with the book propped nimbly under the breastwork of his satchel, prompted word by word.

entities.name: Sargent
entities.body: The boy kept back after class over his sums, ugly and futile, with lean neck and tangled hair and a smear of ink on his cheek, whose mother loved him and who copies the symbols in grave morrice across the page.

entities.name: Sargent’s mother
entities.body: Who taught him to write and bought him a coloured picture book; and who, Stephen thinks, is the only one who loved him and saved him from being trampled underfoot.

entities.name: Halliday
entities.body: On the same side as Cochrane at hockey. Not the Jacob Halliday, vintner, of the mock legal report in episode 12.

entities.name: Curran
entities.body: Ten guineas, in the list of Stephen’s debts. Not John Philpot Curran of episode 7 nor Sara Curran of episode 12.

entities.name: McCann
entities.body: One guinea.

entities.name: Fred Ryan
entities.body: Two shillings.

entities.name: Temple
entities.body: Two lunches — and one of the oval equine faces of Stephen’s dream in episode 3. Not Temple bar.

entities.name: Russell
entities.body: One guinea: George Russell, the eminent poet who signs himself A. E., whom Bloom thinks of in episode 8 and who argues with Stephen in the library in episode 9.

entities.name: Cousins
entities.body: Ten shillings.

entities.name: Bob Reynolds
entities.body: Half a guinea.

entities.name: Koehler
entities.body: Three guineas.

entities.name: Mrs MacKernan
entities.body: Five weeks’ board.

entities.name: Albert Edward, prince of Wales
entities.body: The shapely bulk of a man in tartan fillibegs over Deasy’s mantelpiece, whom he stares at sternly.

entities.name: Sir John Blackwood
entities.body: Deasy’s ancestor, who voted for the union — per vias rectas was his motto — and put on his topboots to ride to Dublin from the Ards of Down to do it. Stephen sees the gruff squire jogging on horseback instead.

entities.name: Mr Henry Blackwood Price
entities.body: Named in Deasy’s letter to the press as making a courteous offer of a fair trial of Koch’s preparation against foot and mouth disease. Not the Henry Price of the basket and fancy goods shop in episode 17.

entities.name: Koch
entities.body: Whose preparation, serum and virus, the letter recommends.

entities.name: lord Hastings|Lord Hastings
entities.body: Owner of Repulse, one of the vanished horses framed on Deasy’s walls.

entities.name: The Duke of Westminster
entities.body: Owner of Shotover, another of them.

entities.name: The Duke of Beaufort
entities.body: Owner of Ceylon, prix de Paris, 1866, the third.

entities.name: O’Connell
entities.body: Whose time Deasy has seen three generations since, and whom the prelates of Stephen’s communion denounced as a demagogue twenty years after the orange lodges had agitated for repeal.

entities.name: Parnell
entities.body: Whom a woman brought low, in Deasy’s list of the women who have ruined men.

entities.name: Edith
entities.body: One of the four faces Stephen watches with envy, whose breaths are sweetened with tea and jam and whose bracelets titter in the struggle.

entities.name: Ethel
entities.body: Another of the four.

entities.name: Gerty
entities.body: A third. Not the Gerty MacDowell of episode 13.

entities.name: Lily
entities.body: The fourth. Not the red Carlisle girl of episode 1, and not the Lily of episodes 6, 12, 13 or 15.

entities.name: Pyrrhus
entities.body: Whose end Armstrong cannot remember and whose fall by a beldam’s hand in Argos Stephen sets beside Caesar’s knifing as one of the things that are not to be thought away. Misled by an oracle, the newspaper men say of him in episode 7, he made a last attempt to retrieve the fortunes of Greece.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.body: Knifed to death: the other of the two actualities Stephen says cannot be thought away.

entities.name: Blake
entities.body: Whose wings of excess thud in Stephen’s thought of history fabled by the daughters of memory, and whose buttocks the creepycrawlers follow into eternity in episode 9. Not the Phil Blake of the weekly Pat and Bull story in episode 7.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: Whose phrase — the soul is the form of forms — forms itself within the gabbled verses and floats out into the studious silence of the library of Saint Genevieve, where Stephen read night by night, sheltered from the sin of Paris.

entities.name: Averroes
entities.body: With Moses Maimonides, one of the dark men in mien and movement, gone from the world, flashing in their mocking mirrors the obscure soul of the world — a darkness shining in brightness which brightness could not comprehend.

entities.name: Moses Maimonides
entities.body: The other of them.

entities.name: Iago
entities.body: Whose line Deasy quotes as Shakespeare’s — put but money in thy purse — and whom Stephen names under his breath in correction.

entities.name: Cassandra
entities.body: The classical allusion Deasy pardons himself for in the letter, and a woman, he adds, who was no better than she should be.

entities.name: Helen
entities.body: The runaway wife of Menelaus, for whom the Greeks made war ten years on Troy — first of Deasy’s women who brought sin into the world.

entities.name: Menelaus
entities.body: Her husband.

entities.name: MacMurrough’s wife
entities.body: The faithless wife who first brought the strangers to our shore here, second of Deasy’s three women who brought sin into the world. The text names her husband only in naming her, and O’Rourke, prince of Breffni, was her leman.

entities.name: O’Rourke, prince of Breffni
entities.body: Her leman.

entities.name: Uncle Richie
entities.body: Richie Goulding, Stephen’s uncle on his mother’s side, in his broad bed with a sturdy forearm over the hillock of his knees, drafting bills of costs on a lapboard and whistling the aria from the opera. He offers Stephen malt, a chippendale chair and a rasher fried with a herring, and admits there is nothing in the house but backache pills. Stephen’s father calls him the drunken little costdrawer. In episode 11 he carries the bag of Goulding, Collis and Ward into the Ormond diningroom, eats steak and kidney across the table from Bloom, cocks his lips to whistle All is lost now, and tells again — a flush struggling in his pale — the night Si Dedalus sang ’Twas rank and fame in Ned Lambert’s house. Coming out with a whopper now, Bloom thinks. Believes his own lies. Does really.

entities.name: Aunt Sara
entities.body: Richie’s wife, and the aunt whose house Stephen is walking towards and then walks past. Stephen’s father calls her aunt Sally and asks whether the boy could not fly a bit higher than Strasburg terrace. She is the mother Walter is sent to for the malt, and she is bathing Crissie when Stephen calls.

entities.name: Walter
entities.body: Richie’s son, skeweyed, who draws the bolt and welcomes Stephen, is sent for the malt, squints vainly for a chair and finds the visitor nothing to sit on. He sirs his own father at every answer, which is what makes Stephen’s father say Jesus wept, and no wonder.

entities.name: Crissie
entities.body: Richie’s small daughter, being bathed upstairs while Stephen stands in the bedroom. Papa’s little bedpal, lump of love.

entities.name: The cornet player
entities.body: Richie’s brother, named in Stephen’s father’s catalogue of the family he married into: the drunken little costdrawer and his brother the cornet player, highly respectable gondoliers.

entities.name: Simon Dedalus
entities.body: Stephen’s father, present in this episode only as the voice in his son’s head — my consubstantial father’s voice — mimicking the Gouldings and asking, and and and and tell us, Stephen, how is uncle Si. In episode 6 he is in the funeral carriage all morning, and from there on every Mr Dedalus and every bare Dedalus in the book is him and not his son. He holds the floor of the newspaper office in episode 7, damns Father Cowley’s landlord on the quay in episode 10, and in episode 11 he walks into the Ormond for a half glass of whisky, is coaxed to the piano by Ben Dollard and Bob Cowley, and sings M’appari to a bar that goes quiet for him. While he sings, the episode calls him Lionel, then Lionel Simon, and at the top note Siopold. Richie Goulding, his brother-in-law, who never speaks to him as they pass by, tells Bloom about another night he sang. Si Dedalus, they call him.

entities.name: Mrs Florence MacCabe
entities.body: One of the two women who come down the steps from Leahy’s terrace and shuffle along the shelving shore, swinging a midwife’s bag. Out from the liberties for the day, of Bride Street. One of her sisterhood lugged Stephen squealing into life, and he wonders what she has in the bag: a misbirth with a trailing navelcord, hushed in ruddy wool.

entities.name: The late Patk MacCabe
entities.body: Her husband, deeply lamented, of Bride Street. The modern edition spells him Patrick.

entities.name: The cocklepicker
entities.body: The man who comes shoreward with a woman and a dog, wades in to souse his bag, calls the dog Tatters off the dead carcass with a blunt bootless kick, and trudges away with the bags shouldered. Blued feet out of turnedup trousers and a dull brick muffler round his unshaven neck. Stephen makes him a ruffian out of the rogues’ lingo.

entities.name: The cocklepicker’s woman
entities.body: Who follows behind her lord with woman steps, spoils slung at her back, loose sand and shellgrit crusted on her bare feet and her hair trailing about her windraw face. Stephen gives her a whole life in three sentences: the archway where dogs have mired, the fancyman treating two Royal Dublins in O’Loughlin’s, Fumbally’s lane and the tanyard smells.

entities.name: The girl at the bookshop window
entities.body: The virgin at Hodges Figgis’ window on Monday, looking in for one of the alphabet books Stephen was going to write, her wrist through the braided jesse of her sunshade. She lives in Leeson park, a lady of letters. The modern edition calls her the young woman at the bookshop window.

entities.name: The two Marys
entities.body: The women who came to the tomb on the third day, and whom Stephen sees in the two figures walking shoreward out of the tide. He adds that they have tucked it safe among the bulrushes, which is Moses and not Easter: the two stories run together in the same breath.

entities.name: Kevin Egan
entities.body: The old Fenian in exile in Paris, rolling gunpowder cigarettes through fingers smeared with printer’s ink and sipping his green fairy, who talks of Ireland and hopes and conspiracies and would yoke Stephen as his yokefellow. Loveless, landless, wifeless, making his day’s stations between the dingy printingcase, his three taverns and the Montmartre lair. They have forgotten Kevin Egan, not he them.

entities.name: Patrice
entities.body: Kevin Egan’s son, home on furlough, who lapped warm milk with Stephen in the bar MacMahon with a plump bunny’s face, hopes to win in the gros lots, read Michelet on the nature of women, and says he is a socialist and does not believe in the existence of God — but his father must not be told. His father calls him Pat: my son, soldier of France.

entities.name: Kevin Egan’s wife
entities.body: The madame in rue Gît-le-Cœur, quite nicey comfy without her outcast man, with a canary and two buck lodgers, peachy cheeks and a zebra skirt, frisky as a young thing.

entities.name: James Stephens
entities.body: The head centre of the Fenian brotherhood, whose escape Kevin Egan retells as the authentic version: got up as a young bride, man, veil, orangeblossoms, and driven out the road to Malahide. Episode 3 names him only by his office — the modern edition calls him the rebel leader — and Bloom gives him his name at 4:159: the chap in the paybox at the Tara street baths got away James Stephens, they say. Not the James Stephens of 9:126, who is doing some clever sketches.

entities.name: The froeken
entities.body: The Swedish maid of all work who rubs male nakedness in the bath at Upsala — it is my job, she said, all the gentlemen — in Egan’s account of most licentious custom. The modern edition calls her the Scandinavian girl.

entities.name: Esther Osvalt
entities.body: The girl Stephen knew in Paris, whose shoe went on his foot: what a pretty little foot. He remembers being delighted by it while looking down at another man’s castoff boots on his own feet.

entities.name: Belluomo
entities.body: Who rises from the bed of his wife’s lover’s wife in Stephen’s Paris waking rawly. The name is Italian for a handsome man, and the modern edition prints the translation in place of the name.

entities.name: Yvonne
entities.body: One of the two women in Rodot’s who newmake their tumbled beauties, shattering chaussons of pastry with gold teeth, their mouths yellowed with flan.

entities.name: Madeleine
entities.body: The other of them. Not Madeline the mare of the song at the start of the episode, who is a horse and is spelt with an i.

entities.name: Arthur Griffith
entities.body: Named in Egan’s talk of hopes and conspiracies, beside A E and the good shepherd of men. Bloom thinks of him twice in the course of the day: the man who said the thing about the homerule sun rising up in the northwest, and a squareheaded fellow with no go in him for the mob.

entities.name: Monsieur Drumont
entities.body: The famous French journalist Egan quotes, who called queen Victoria an old hag with the yellow teeth. Stephen gives the phrase back to himself later on the strand, with his own bad teeth in his mouth.

entities.name: Queen Victoria
entities.body: The old hag with the yellow teeth, in Drumont’s phrase, which Stephen repeats. She had been dead three years on the day of this book.

entities.name: Maud Gonne
entities.body: Beautiful woman, in Egan’s roll of Paris names. Bloom remembers her letter about taking the soldiers off O’Connell street at night: disgrace to our Irish capital.

entities.name: Monsieur Millevoye
entities.body: The French journalist and politician named beside Maud Gonne in the same breath, with La Patrie between them.

entities.name: Félix Faure
entities.body: Named next, with the question Egan leaves hanging: know how he died? The answer is the two words that follow — licentious men.

entities.name: Brian Boru
entities.body: The high king whose warriors Egan means when he talks of Ireland. He is on the citizen’s girdle in episode 12 as Brian of Kincora, third among the tribal images. The older edition calls them the Dalcassians, which is the name of his people and not of a man; the modern edition puts the king in place of the people, so this card exists in the modern edition alone.

entities.name: Colonel Richard Burke
entities.body: Tanist of his sept, with whom Egan prowled under the walls of Clerkenwell and, crouching, saw a flame of vengeance hurl them upward in the fog. Not the O’Madden Burke of the newspaper office, nor Pisser Burke of the City Arms, nor Burke’s public house.

entities.name: Napper Tandy
entities.body: Who takes me by the hand in the song Egan sings out of The Wearing of the Green. Not the Shapland Tandy whose bills of costs uncle Richie drafts.

entities.name: Master Shapland Tandy
entities.body: One of the two masters for whose eyes Richie Goulding drafts his bills of costs, with master Goff, among consents and common searches and a writ of Duces Tecum. Not Napper Tandy of the song.

entities.name: Master Goff
entities.body: The other of the two, named in the same line of legal work.

entities.name: Strongbow
entities.body: Whose castle on the Nore stands over old Kilkenny in Egan’s memory of the song he taught Patrice.

entities.name: Saint Canice
entities.body: Of Kilkenny, named with Strongbow’s castle in the same memory, and again in the long procession of saints in episode 12.

entities.name: Los Demiurgos
entities.body: The maker whose mallet Stephen hears in the solid sound of his own boots on the strand. The modern edition replaces the demiurge of the gnostics with God the Creator.

entities.name: Adam
entities.body: The first man: Adam Kadmon, the primal man of the kabbalists, whose spouse and helpmate is Heva; and again, at the end of the episode, unfallen Adam who rode and did not rut. The modern edition writes the primal man Adam.

entities.name: Eve
entities.body: Heva, naked Eve, who had no navel — belly without blemish, a buckler of taut vellum — set against the trailing navelcord in the midwife’s bag. The older edition gives her Hebrew name first; the modern edition drops it and keeps Eve.

entities.name: Mananaan
entities.body: Mananaan MacLir, the Irish sea god, whose steeds are the whitemaned seahorses of the waves coming in. The modern edition explains him as the sea god Mananaan; A E invokes him by both names in the library.

entities.name: Joachim Abbas
entities.body: The abbot whose fading prophecies Stephen read in the stagnant bay of Marsh’s library, and whom Mulligan mocks in episode 10 as mumbling Joachim. The modern edition names him Joachim of Fiore.

entities.name: Foxy Campbell
entities.body: One of the oval equine faces in Stephen’s procession of the mad: Temple, Buck Mulligan, Foxy Campbell, Lanternjaws. Not the Thomas Campbell of the churchyard poem, nor Henry Campbell the townclerk.

entities.name: Lanternjaws
entities.body: The last of the four faces, known by his jaw and by nothing else. The modern edition hyphenates him.

entities.name: Dan Occam
entities.body: The invincible doctor, who thought of the host elevated in two churches at once — a misty English morning, the imp hypostasis tickled his brain. The modern edition names him William of Ockham and calls him the invincible logician.

entities.name: The Blessed Virgin
entities.body: To whom Stephen prayed that he might not have a red nose, in the same breath in which he prayed to the devil in Serpentine avenue that the fubsy widow in front might lift her clothes still more.

entities.name: Pico della Mirandola
entities.body: Whom Stephen thinks of over the epiphanies he meant to have sent, if he died, to all the great libraries of the world, including Alexandria: someone was to read them there after a few thousand years. Ay, very like a whale.

entities.name: Michelet
entities.body: The French historian in whom Patrice read about the nature of women, over warm milk in the bar MacMahon.

entities.name: Monsieur Léo Taxil
entities.body: Author of La Vie de Jésus, which Patrice must send Stephen and has lent to a friend. His is the joke of the pigeon — who put you in this wretched position? It was the pigeon, Joseph — and the French of it comes back in episode 14.

entities.name: Columbanus
entities.body: The fiery missionary to Europe Stephen meant to follow, and who in the history lesson of the episode before bestrode his own mother’s prostrate body in holy zeal. The modern edition calls him Saint Columban.

entities.name: Fiacre
entities.body: One of the two Irish monks laughing in heaven on their creepystools, spilt from their pintpots. Not the church of Saint Fiacre in Horto of the mock wedding report in episode 12.

entities.name: Scotus
entities.body: The other of them, loudlatinlaughing: Euge! Euge!

entities.name: Malachi
entities.body: The high king who wore the collar of gold, in Stephen’s vision of the Danish galleys beaching on this same strand. The ardri Malachi of the roll of Irish heroes in episode 12 is the same king. Malachi Mulligan is not, and neither is the Saint Malachy of the procession.

entities.name: The Bruce’s brother
entities.body: Edward Bruce, brother of Robert the Bruce, crowned king of Ireland and killed for it: first of Stephen’s four pretenders. The text names him only as his brother’s brother.

entities.name: Thomas Fitzgerald
entities.body: Silken Thomas, the silken knight, second of the four. Not the lord Edward Fitzgerald who escaped from major Sirr, nor the Fitzgerald Mor, the great earl.

entities.name: Perkin Warbeck
entities.body: York’s false scion, in breeches of silk of whiterose ivory, wonder of a day.

entities.name: Lambert Simnel
entities.body: With a tail of nans and sutlers, a scullion crowned. Last of the four, and the one the thought closes on: all kings’ sons, paradise of pretenders then and now.

entities.name: Guido
entities.body: Whom the courtiers mocked in Or san Michele — and they were in their own house, which is the turn Stephen uses against himself while deciding he would not go in after a drowning man. The modern edition calls him the poet Guido and drops the name of the church.

entities.name: Sir Lout
entities.body: The giant whose toys are the stoneheaps on the strand: I am the bloody well gigant rolls all them bloody well boulders, bones for my steppingstones. Feefawfum. The modern edition keeps the giant and drops the name.

entities.name: Haroun al Raschid
entities.body: The caliph of the dream Stephen is almosting: open hallway, street of harlots, the man who led me and held a melon against my face, and the red carpet spread. The modern edition adds that he is out of the Arabian Nights and spells him Rashid.

entities.name: Louis Veuillot
entities.body: Who called Gautier’s prose a coach stuck in the sand — the phrase Stephen turns over on these heavy sands. The modern edition explains him as the French critic.

entities.name: Théophile Gautier
entities.body: Whose prose he called it. The older edition gives the surname alone; the modern edition supplies the first name.

entities.name: Ferrando
entities.body: Whose aria di sortita uncle Richie drones on his padded knees: the grandest number, Stephen, in the whole opera. The modern edition spells him Fernando.

entities.name: Saint Ambrose
entities.body: Who heard the sigh of leaves and waves waiting and awaiting the fullness of their times, in the Latin Stephen quotes over the weeds swaying under the tide.

entities.name: The bishop of Cloyne
entities.body: Who took the veil of the temple out of his shovel hat: the veil of space with coloured emblems hatched on its field. The modern edition names him, calling him the philosopher Bishop Berkeley and giving him a top hat.

entities.name: Pan
entities.body: Whose hour is the faunal noon in which Stephen lies back over the sharp rocks with his hat tilted down on his eyes, among gumheavy serpentplants and milkoozing fruits.

entities.name: Lawn Tennyson
entities.body: Gentleman poet, whose May Queen gives Stephen the line he hums with his bad teeth — of all the glad new year, mother, the rum tum tiddledy tum. The same phrase for him comes back in the library in episode 9.

entities.name: Lucifer
entities.body: Allbright he falls, proud lightning of the intellect. The Latin Stephen quotes is from the Easter Exsultet, where Lucifer is the morning star that knows no setting; Stephen means the falling angel as well.

entities.name: Leopold Bloom
entities.body: The man the book follows from this morning to the small hours: an advertisement canvasser of 7 Eccles street who eats with relish the inner organs of beasts and fowls, fries a pork kidney for his own breakfast and carries his wife her tea in bed. Jewish by descent in a city that will not let him forget it, kind to the cat, curious about everything, and carrying a potato in his pocket. His wife calls him Poldy and his daughter calls him Papli.

entities.name: Molly Bloom
entities.body: Marion Bloom, born Marion Tweedy at Gibraltar: a concert soprano, and in bed for the whole of this episode, reading a novel and asking her husband what metempsychosis means. Tell us in plain words. The letter in the bold hand that she glances at and tucks under the pillow is from Blazes Boylan, who is coming at four with the programme. The envelope calls her Mrs Marion Bloom, which is not how a letter is addressed to a married woman.

entities.name: Milly Bloom
entities.body: Their daughter, fifteen yesterday and away from home for the first time, learning the photography business at Mullingar. Her birthday letter thanks her father for the present, says everyone says she is quite the belle in her new tam, and mentions a young student named Bannon who sings Boylan’s song about those seaside girls. Her father calls her silly Milly; she signs herself your fond daughter Milly.

entities.name: Rudy
entities.body: Their son, who lived eleven days. Mrs Thornton knew from the first that he would not live, and knew at once. He would be eleven now if he had lived, and the thought of him runs under everything his father does in this book.

entities.name: Old Tweedy
entities.body: Molly’s father, who bought the bed at the governor’s auction at Gibraltar and got a short knock — hard as nails at a bargain, and I rose from the ranks, sir, and I’m proud of it. He made a corner in stamps, which Bloom calls farseeing, and his big moustaches walk into the daydream of the east. The modern edition calls him old Major Tweedy.

entities.name: Hanlon’s milkman
entities.body: Who had just filled the jug Bloom pours the cat’s milk out of. The modern edition drops the dairy’s name and leaves only the milkman.

entities.name: Larry O’Rourke
entities.body: The publican on the corner, a cute old codger and baldhead over the blind, leaning against the sugarbin in his shirtsleeves and watching the curate swab up. No use canvassing him for an ad, but he knows his own business best. Bloom says good day through the doorway and thinks of stopping to say a word about the funeral. Simon Dedalus takes him off to a tee with his eyes screwed up.

entities.name: Dlugacz
entities.body: The ferreteyed porkbutcher of Dorset street with a deep voice, blotchy sausagepink fingers and a pile of cut sheets from a Zionist planting company to wrap the sausages in. Bloom buys the last pork kidney from him and carries away one of the sheets. A later episode gives him a first name: Moses Dlugacz.

entities.name: The nextdoor girl
entities.body: The servant from the house next door, at the counter ahead of Bloom with a slip in her hand and a pound and a half of Denny’s sausages. The porkbutcher calls her my miss; Bloom means to catch up and walk behind her and does not, and thinks of the constable off duty who cuddles her in Eccles lane. She is in the next garden again when he goes down to the jakes.

entities.name: Woods
entities.body: The neighbour she works for. Woods his name is: wonder what he does, wife is oldish, no followers allowed.

entities.name: Blazes Boylan
entities.body: Who is bringing Molly the programme at four, and whose letter in the bold hand goes under her pillow unread in front of her husband. Bloom will not hold the name in his mind for long at a time: is that Boylan well off, he has money, why, I noticed he had a good rich smell off his breath dancing. Milly writes that the young student sings Boylan’s song about those seaside girls, and nearly writes Blazes.

entities.name: Mr Coghlan
entities.body: The photographer Milly works for at Mullingar, who took one of her and Mrs and will send it when developed.

entities.name: Professor Goodwin
entities.body: Molly’s old accompanist, a dreadful old case and a courteous old chap, who used to bow her off the platform in the oldfashioned way and kept a little mirror in his silk hat. Milly found it and carried it into the parlour, and they all laughed.

entities.name: Dignam
entities.body: Whose funeral is at eleven, and the fixed point of the day for half the men in this book. Bloom comes back to him three times before he has left the house: a word about him to Larry O’Rourke, a man’s soul after he dies — Dignam’s soul — and, under the bells of George’s church, poor Dignam. Not Master Patrick Aloysius Dignam of episode 10, who is his son.

entities.name: Mrs Thornton
entities.body: The midwife of Denzille street, a jolly old woman who must have helped a lot of babies into the world, whom Bloom ran to knock up the summer morning Milly was born, and who knew from the first that Rudy would not live. Well, God is good, sir.

entities.name: Citron
entities.body: Of Saint Kevin’s parade, in whose basketchair Molly used to sit on the pleasant evenings of the old Lombard street days. Wonder is poor Citron still there.

entities.name: Mastiansky
entities.body: Of the same evenings, with the old cither, and the man who told Bloom that the giant poppies of the Chinese cemeteries produce the best opium. A later episode gives him a first name, Julius; the Mrs Mastiansky of the last episode is his wife and not him.

entities.name: Moisel
entities.body: Who told Bloom that the citrons fetched high prices too. Arbutus place, Pleasants street: pleasant old times.

entities.name: The Norwegian captain
entities.body: Whose back Bloom is reminded of by a man on the quayside he knows just to salute — chap you know just to salute, bit of a bore. The captain is not described and is named nowhere else in the book in these words.

entities.name: Adam Findlater
entities.body: One of two Dublin names Bloom uses as a type: the redheaded curates up from the county Leitrim, rinsing empties, who then lo and behold blossom out as Adam Findlaters or Dan Tallons. The modern edition drops both names and writes successful businessmen instead, so this card exists in the older edition alone.

entities.name: Dan Tallon
entities.body: The other of the two. The modern edition drops him here as well, but keeps him at 17:109, where he is the new lord mayor, Daniel Tallon.

entities.name: Moses Montefiore
entities.body: Whose name stands on the sheet Bloom takes from the porkbutcher’s pile, over the model farm at Kinnereth on the lakeshore of Tiberias. I thought he was, Bloom says, and leaves the sentence unfinished.

entities.name: Kearney
entities.body: Bloom’s guarantor at the Capel street library, who will be written to if the book is not renewed. Not the Kathleen Kearney whom Molly cannot bear.

entities.name: M’Coy
entities.body: Through whom Bloom thinks he might work a press pass to Mullingar, to go down and see Milly. He appears in person in the next episode and asks to have his name put down at the funeral. The modern edition spells him McCoy from episode 8 on.

entities.name: Gretta Conroy
entities.body: Whose dress Molly asked about at 9.20 one morning while she dressed — one of the remarks Bloom used to try jotting down on his cuff.

entities.name: Sandow
entities.body: Whose exercises Bloom must begin again. On the hands down. A later episode names the book: Eugen Sandow, Physical Strength and How to Obtain It.

entities.name: Ponchielli
entities.body: Whose dance of the hours May’s band played the morning after the bazaar dance, and which Bloom is still explaining to himself: morning hours, noon, then evening coming on, then night hours.

entities.name: J. C. Doyle
entities.body: The singer Molly is to sing Là ci darem with on the tour, with Love’s Old Sweet Song for the other number.

entities.name: Katey Keogh
entities.body: With her ass and garden, in the song Bloom sings over his daughter’s letter: I’d rather have you without a farthing than Katey Keogh.

entities.name: Paul de Kock
entities.body: The French novelist Molly wants another of. Nice name he has — which is the whole of Bloom’s comment, and enough.

entities.name: Ruby
entities.body: The pride of the ring, on the floor naked in the illustration with the sheet kindly lent: the heroine of the novel Molly has finished and wants replaced. The first Ruby on the page is the title of the book and carries no card; the second is the girl.

entities.name: Maffei
entities.body: The monster who desisted and flung his victim from him with an oath — the fierce Italian with the carriagewhip in the illustration.

entities.name: Mr Philip Beaufoy
entities.body: Of the Playgoers’ Club, London, who wrote Matcham’s Masterstroke and was paid at the rate of one guinea a column for it. Bloom reads it seated calm above his own rising smell, envies him kindly the three pounds thirteen and six, and tears away half of it to wipe himself. Not the Mrs Beaufoy of episode 8, who is Mrs Purefoy under a slip of the tongue.

entities.name: Matcham
entities.body: Who often thinks of the masterstroke by which he won the laughing witch who now. Begins and ends morally. Hand in hand. Smart. His story stands in Gutenberg italics in the older edition, which is why his name is keyed and not aliased.

entities.name: Henry Flower
entities.body: The name Bloom writes under and collects his letters under: Henry Flower Esq, care of the post office in Westland row. He carries the card for it behind the leather headband of his hat and puts it back before going into church. It is his own name translated — Virag, his father’s name, is Hungarian for flower.

entities.name: Martha
entities.body: The typist who writes to Henry Flower and signs herself Martha: I called you naughty boy because I do not like that other world. Please tell me what is the real meaning of that word. She pins a yellow flower to the letter and asks, in a postscript, what perfume his wife uses. Her surname, Clifford, is given in a later episode.

entities.name: The postmistress
entities.body: Who searches the pigeonhole at Westland row and hands Bloom back his card with a letter, while he holds his rolled newspaper against his nostrils and looks at the recruiting poster.

entities.name: Mrs M’Coy
entities.body: Whose engagement is not settled yet: a reedy freckled soprano with a cheeseparing nose, nice enough for a little ballad. Her husband brings her up so as to borrow a valise, which is the wheeze Bloom did not fall for.

entities.name: Bantam Lyons
entities.body: Who takes Bloom’s newspaper at his armpit with yellow blacknailed fingers to look up the French horse running at Ascot, hears him say twice that he was going to throw it away, and speeds off towards Conway’s corner to back Throwaway. Bloom never learns what he has said.

entities.name: Bob Doran
entities.body: On one of his periodical bends, in Conway’s with Bantam Lyons when M’Coy was there.

entities.name: Hoppy Holohan
entities.body: Who told M’Coy about the funeral, and came into Conway’s for a wet. You know Hoppy?

entities.name: Corny Kelleher
entities.body: Who Bloom daresays bagged the funeral job for O’Neill’s, singing with his eyes shut. Police tout, he adds, and goes off into the tooraloom song. He manages the undertaker’s, and turns up wherever the day’s business is.

entities.name: Tom Kernan
entities.body: The tea traveller, from whom Bloom means to get tea and cannot ask at a funeral. He struts into the Ormond in episode 11 in the middle of the singing, tells the authentic fact of how Walter Bapty lost his voice, overrules Qui sdegno in favour of The Croppy Boy — our native Doric — and pronounces the result most trenchant, upon my soul and honour it is. The episode calls him Tomgin.

entities.name: Hornblower
entities.body: At the porter’s lodge of Trinity, worth keeping on hands: might take a turn in there on the nod. How do you do, Mr Hornblower? How do you do, sir?

entities.name: The chemist
entities.body: Of Sweny’s in Lincoln place, who turns back page after page of the prescriptions book to find the lotion of sweet almond oil and tincture of benzoin, and sells Bloom a cake of sweet lemony soap for fourpence to be paid for later. Sandy shrivelled smell he seems to have. Shrunken skull. And old.

entities.name: The boy for the skins
entities.body: Lolling by Brady’s cottages with his bucket of offal linked, smoking a chewed fagbutt. Tell him if he smokes he won’t grow. O let him. His life isn’t such a bed of roses.

entities.name: The girl with the caskhoop
entities.body: Smaller, with scars of eczema on her forehead, who eyes him listlessly, holding her battered hoop.

entities.name: The two in the Coombe
entities.body: The two women linked together in the rain that night in the Coombe, whose flat Dublin voices bawl the song about Mairy’s drawers in Bloom’s head, and who would listen too, he thinks, in the house at Bethany. The modern edition calls them two rough girls.

entities.name: Poor papa
entities.body: Bloom’s father, who used to talk of Kate Bateman in Leah and of the scene where the old blind Abraham knows his son’s voice. Episode 12 gives him his names at last, and gives them against his son: old Methusalem Bloom the robbing bagman, who swamped the country with baubles and penny diamonds on loans by post and poisoned himself with prussic acid; Virag, says Martin Cunningham, the father’s name, changed by deedpoll; and Nagyaságos uram Lipóti Virag of Messrs Alexander Thom’s, seen off to the Meadow of Murmuring Waters by a large and appreciative gathering in the last parody but one. He is not named in this episode, and Bloom is glad he did not go into the room to look at his face. That day. O, dear! O, dear!

entities.name: Bob Cowley
entities.body: Father Cowley, barricaded up against his landlord, who lent M’Coy his valise for the Wicklow regatta concert last year and never heard tidings of it from that good day to this. In episode 11 he accompanies from the Ormond piano — the way he sits in to it, Bloom thinks, like one together, mutual understanding — plays Simon Dedalus in on M’appari and Ben Dollard through The Croppy Boy, and stuns himself with it: kind of drunkenness.

entities.name: Vance
entities.body: The High school master who cracked his fingerjoints teaching the law of falling bodies: thirtytwo feet per second per second. He taught the colours of the spectrum too.

entities.name: Mrs Ellis
entities.body: Who kept the old dame’s school where Bloom played marbles, and liked mignonette. And Mr? — the question he leaves unfinished.

entities.name: Jack Fleming
entities.body: Who embezzled to gamble and was smuggled off to America, and keeps a hotel now. They never come back.

entities.name: Captain Culler
entities.body: Who broke a window in the Kildare street club with a slog to square leg — the whole of Bloom’s case for cricket in Ireland.

entities.name: M’Carthy
entities.body: Whose taking the floor set the skulls cracking, in the song Bloom half quotes about Donnybrook fair. Not the Jakes M’Carthy of episode 7, nor Justin M’Carthy, nor Denis Florence M’Carthy.

entities.name: Mairy
entities.body: Who lost the pin of her drawers and did not know what to do to keep it up, in the song of the two women in the Coombe. The modern edition spells her Mary.

entities.name: Martin Cunningham
entities.body: Who knows Father Conmee. He is the organiser of the funeral party in the next episode and of the collection for the Dignams after it.

entities.name: Father John Conmee
entities.body: Whose sermon on saint Peter Claver and the African Mission is on the notice at the door of All Hallows. Distinguishedlooking, Bloom thinks, and regrets not having worked him about getting Molly into the choir. He opens episode 10 walking across Dublin.

entities.name: Saint Peter Claver
entities.body: The Jesuit of the African mission, subject of the sermon — and the name Bloom reaches for and mixes up with Peter Carey, a few paragraphs later, in the same church.

entities.name: Gladstone
entities.body: For whose conversion they had prayers when he was almost unconscious. The protestants are the same, Bloom adds.

entities.name: Dr William J. Walsh
entities.body: Archbishop of Dublin, whom the protestants would convert to the true religion in the same way. Not the Louis J Walsh of Magherafelt in episode 13.

entities.name: Father Farley
entities.body: Who got the choir place instead of Molly, and who looked a fool but wasn’t.

entities.name: Carey
entities.body: The informer who turned queen’s evidence on the invincibles and took communion every morning in this very church, with a wife and six children at home and the murder plotted all the while. Bloom cannot fix the first name: Carey was his name, Peter Carey, yes — no, Peter Claver I am thinking of — Denis Carey. Episode 8 has him hesitating the same way: Peter or Denis or James Carey.

entities.name: Old Glynn
entities.body: The organist of Gardiner street, who knew how to make that instrument talk, the vibrato, and had fifty pounds a year for it.

entities.name: Father Bernard Vaughan
entities.body: Whose sermon came before the music on the day Molly was in fine voice: Christ or Pilate? Christ, but don’t keep us all night over it.

entities.name: Mrs Bandmann Palmer
entities.body: Playing Leah tonight, and Hamlet last night: a male impersonator, which sets Bloom wondering whether Hamlet was a woman and why Ophelia committed suicide.

entities.name: Kate Bateman
entities.body: Whom Bloom’s father used to talk of in the same part, and waited all the afternoon outside the Adelphi in London to see — the year before Bloom was born, sixtyfive.

entities.name: Ristori
entities.body: And Ristori in Vienna: the other actress his father named.

entities.name: Mosenthal
entities.body: Who wrote the play. By Mosenthal it is. Bloom gropes for the title after the author’s name and does not find it.

entities.name: Nathan
entities.body: Whose voice the old blind man knows in the scene Bloom’s father was always talking about: Nathan’s voice! His son’s voice! I hear the voice of Nathan who left his father to die of grief and misery in my arms.

entities.name: Abraham
entities.body: The old blind man of that scene, who recognises the voice and puts his fingers on his face. Not the patriarch of episodes 12 and 15.

entities.name: Ophelia
entities.body: Who committed suicide, and why — the question Bloom asks himself in front of the playbill, and which the library argument of episode 9 takes up in earnest.

entities.name: Pilate
entities.body: Christ or Pilate, the choice Father Bernard Vaughan’s sermon offered. Professor MacHugh gives him a second line in episode 7.

entities.name: Saint Michael
entities.body: The archangel of the prayer after mass: blessed Michael, defend us in the hour of conflict. His host are the embattled angels of the church whose menace Stephen remembers in episode 1.

entities.name: Satan
entities.body: Whom the same prayer asks God to thrust down to hell, with those other wicked spirits who wander through the world for the ruin of souls.

entities.name: Saint Peter
entities.body: Named with Paul in Bloom’s inventory of what the mass is about: glorious and immaculate virgin, Joseph her spouse, Peter and Paul.

entities.name: Saint Paul
entities.body: The other of the pair.

entities.name: Buddha
entities.body: Lying on his side in the museum with his hand under his cheek, taking it easy, josssticks burning: the god Bloom sets against the Ecce Homo, the crown of thorns and the cross.

entities.name: Mohammed
entities.body: Who cut a piece out of his mantle rather than wake the cat asleep on it — the story Bloom remembers over a tabby on a warm sill. The modern edition calls him the Prophet Muhammad.

entities.name: Saint Patrick
entities.body: And the shamrock: clever idea, Bloom says, in the same breath as the chopsticks and the heathen Chinee.

entities.name: Lord Iveagh
entities.body: Who once cashed a sevenfigure cheque for a million in the bank of Ireland. Shows you the money to be made out of porter.

entities.name: Lord Ardilaun
entities.body: The other brother, who has to change his shirt four times a day, they say.

entities.name: The duke of Albany
entities.body: One of the old queen’s sons, who had only one skin. Leopold, yes — which is Bloom’s own name, and the only reason he remembers the man.

entities.name: Brutus
entities.body: And Brutus is an honourable man: Antony’s line, which Bloom turns on the stylish woman outside the Grosvenor. The honourable Mrs.

entities.name: Rossini
entities.body: Whose Stabat Mater Molly sang in Gardiner street, with the thrill in the air and the people looking up.

entities.name: Mercadante
entities.body: Of the seven last words, first of Bloom’s list of that old sacred music, splendid. Molly sang his Quis est homo too.

entities.name: Mozart
entities.body: Whose twelfth mass has the Gloria in it.

entities.name: Palestrina
entities.body: For example too, among the old popes keen on music and art and statues and pictures of all kinds. They had a gay old time while it lasted.

entities.name: Martha and Mary
entities.body: The two sisters of Bethany, one of whom walks the procession of saints in episode 12 as S. Martha of Bethany, and in whose house Christ sat talking — the picture Bloom half remembers when his correspondent’s name slides into the gospel: old master or faked for money. He is sitting in their house, talking. Mysterious.

entities.name: The old woman peeping
entities.body: Who drags her blind aside as the funeral leaves Newbridge avenue, her nose whiteflattened against the pane, thanking her stars she was passed over. Extraordinary the interest they take in a corpse, Bloom thinks: glad to see us go, we give them such trouble coming.

entities.name: Mr Power
entities.body: Jack Power, the fourth man in the carriage: goodlooking, greyish over the ears, and the one who says out loud that the worst of all is the man who takes his own life, not knowing whose father did. Bloom has heard he keeps a barmaid from Jury’s or the Moira. Mr Dedalus calls him Jack at the graveside.

entities.name: Mrs Fleming
entities.body: Who comes in to clean at Eccles street, made the bed with Molly, and did not darn Bloom’s socks well enough.

entities.name: Ignatius Gallaher
entities.body: With whom Richie Goulding waltzed in Stamer street of a Sunday morning, the landlady’s two hats pinned on his head. The newspaper men of episode 7 remember him as the man who paralysed Europe.

entities.name: Peter Paul M’Swiney
entities.body: Mr Dedalus’s cousin, in whose shop a counterjumper’s son sold tapes — the whole of his case against Mulligan.

entities.name: Ned Lambert
entities.body: One of the mourners behind, who was down for the Cork park races and stopped with Dick Tivy, tells Mr Dedalus who is walking in front, and tells John Henry Menton who Bloom is.

entities.name: Hynes
entities.body: The reporter, who walks behind with Ned Lambert and takes the names at the graveside for the paper — and takes down M’Intosh as a name because Bloom said macintosh. He asks the others to go round by the chief’s grave.

entities.name: Paddy Leonard
entities.body: Who was taking Tom Kernan off to his face last night.

entities.name: Ben Dollard
entities.body: Big Ben, base barreltone: a ships’ chandler once, failed to the tune of ten thousand pounds and now in the Iveagh home, who in episode 11 pushes Father Cowley into the Ormond saloon, plumps himself on the stool with his gouty paws, bawls Love and War, and is talked into The Croppy Boy in F sharp major. Tom Kernan calls it the most trenchant rendition of that ballad, upon his soul and honour; the bar chinks glasses to him afterwards, Benaben, Benben.

entities.name: Dan Dawson
entities.body: Whose speech is in the paper this morning, and which Mr Dedalus refuses to have read out to him in a carriage. The newspaper office takes it apart in episode 7.

entities.name: Eugene Stratton
entities.body: On the hoardings past the Queen’s theatre, and on them again for Father Conmee in episode 10.

entities.name: Sir Philip Crampton
entities.body: Whose memorial fountain bust they pass. Who was he? — which is the whole of Bloom’s thought about him.

entities.name: Mary Anderson
entities.body: Who is up in Belfast now, in Martin Cunningham’s one contribution to the talk about the concert tour.

entities.name: Louis Werner
entities.body: Who is touring Molly.

entities.name: John MacCormack
entities.body: Whom Bloom hopes to have among the topnobbers, with J. C. Doyle.

entities.name: Smith O’Brien
entities.body: Whose statue has a bunch of flowers laid at it. Must be his deathday, Bloom thinks: for many happy returns.

entities.name: O’Callaghan
entities.body: The old man at the curbstone selling four bootlaces for a penny, struck off the rolls, who had his office in Hume street and has had the silk hat ever since. Relics of old decency. On his last legs.

entities.name: Tweedy, crown solicitor for Waterford
entities.body: Molly’s namesake, who had his office in the same house. Not her father.

entities.name: Crofton
entities.body: Who met Mr Power one evening bringing his woman a pound of rumpsteak — the only evidence Bloom has for the story. He comes into Barney Kiernan’s in episode 12 on the castle car with Martin Cunningham and Jack Power, a pensioner out of the collector general’s and an orangeman or presbyterian, and nobody there can settle his name: a fellow named Crofter or Crofton, or Crawford, in one sentence. No offence, Crofton.

entities.name: Sir John Gray
entities.body: Whose statue the carriage passes while Mr Power collapses in laughter.

entities.name: Nelson
entities.body: Whose pillar they pass. Horatio onehandled Nelson, as episode 11 has him.

entities.name: Father Mathew
entities.body: The temperance apostle, under whose patronage the dead side of the street stands, with the foundation stone for Parnell beside it.

entities.name: Reuben J
entities.body: Reuben J Dodd, the moneylender, stumping round the corner of Elvery’s on a stick — of the tribe of Reuben, Martin Cunningham says, and the carriage enjoys him. He gave the boatman who fished his son out of the Liffey a florin, which Mr Dedalus calls one and eightpence too much. Mr Dedalus also calls him Barabbas, after the robber released instead of Christ, and does so again in episode 10.

entities.name: Reuben J’s son
entities.body: The young chiseller, whom his father was sending to the Isle of Man out of harm’s way over a girl, and who got loose on the quay and went over the wall into the river.

entities.name: The boatman
entities.body: Who got a pole and fished him out by the slack of the breeches and landed him up to the father more dead than alive. Half the town was there. A silver florin.

entities.name: John Henry Menton
entities.body: Solicitor, commissioner for oaths and affidavits, in whose office Dignam used to be. He danced with Molly at Mat Dillon’s seventeen golden years ago and has disliked Bloom ever since an evening at bowls, and asks Ned Lambert in God’s name what she married a coon like that for. Bloom points out the dinge in his hat and gets a short thank you.

entities.name: Mat Dillon
entities.body: Jolly Mat of Roundtown, in whose house Molly and Menton danced: convivial evenings, cold fowl, cigars, the Tantalus glasses. Heart of gold really.

entities.name: Floey Dillon
entities.body: Linked with Molly under the lilactree, laughing, on the same evening.

entities.name: Wisdom Hely
entities.body: The stationer Bloom travelled for, in blottingpaper.

entities.name: Dick Tivy
entities.body: The solid man of Cork, with whom Ned Lambert stopped for the races, and who has nothing between himself and heaven — which is Ned Lambert’s way of saying he is bald.

entities.name: The boy with the wreath
entities.body: Paddy Dignam’s eldest, in a brandnew collar, sleekcombed, who carries one of the two wreaths, is beckoned to kneel by Corny Kelleher, and stands at the gravehead holding it with both hands. Martin Cunningham is trying to get him into Artane. He has episode 10 to himself, carrying home a pound and a half of porksteaks.

entities.name: The brother-in-law
entities.body: Who walks beside the boy, carries the other wreath, and at the end places something in the gravedigger’s free hand.

entities.name: Dignam’s wife
entities.body: Left with five young children and a policy heavily mortgaged. A great blow to the poor wife, Mr Kernan says, and Bloom thinks: she had outlived him.

entities.name: Father Coffey
entities.body: Who reads the service over the coffin in a fluent croak. I knew his name was like a coffin, Bloom thinks: bully about the muzzle, bosses the show, with a belly on him like a poisoned pup. Not the Coffey the butcher of episode 8.

entities.name: The server
entities.body: The boy who carries the brass bucket in before the priest, pipes the answers in the treble, and holds the bucket while the priest shakes the thing over the coffin.

entities.name: Mervyn Browne
entities.body: Who told Bloom that down in the vaults of saint Werburgh’s they have to bore a hole in the coffins sometimes to let out the bad gas.

entities.name: John O’Connell
entities.body: The caretaker of Glasnevin: a portly man ambushed among the grasses who never forgets a friend, shakes all their hands in silence, and tells the story of the two drunks and Mulcahy from the Coombe. Keys at his back, and a prosperous bulk Bloom admires. Not Daniel O’Connell, whose circle they are standing in.

entities.name: Terence Mulcahy
entities.body: From the Coombe, whose grave the two drunks found in the fog, and whose widow had put up a statue of Our Saviour over it. Not a bloody bit like the man, said the second drunk. That’s not Mulcahy, whoever done it.

entities.name: Mulcahy’s widow
entities.body: Who had the statue put up.

entities.name: Major Gamble
entities.body: Who calls Mount Jerome his garden — the protestant cemetery on the other side of the city.

entities.name: Spurgeon
entities.body: Of the caretaker’s other joke, the one about the bulletin: Spurgeon went to heaven 4 a.m. this morning. 11 p.m. (closing time). Not arrived yet. Peter.

entities.name: M’Intosh
entities.body: The thirteenth man at the graveside, a lankylooking galoot in a macintosh who was not in the chapel and whom nobody knows. Bloom says the word for the coat; Hynes writes it down as a name, and it is the name he keeps for the rest of the book.

entities.name: Louis Byrne
entities.body: Under whom M’Coy got the job in the morgue after the Freeman.

entities.name: Cuffe
entities.body: Who sold the cattle at about twentyseven quid each. Bloom worked for him once, and was given the order of the boot for it.

entities.name: James M’Cann
entities.body: Whose hobby is developing the waterways — to row me o’er the ferry. Not the McCann of Stephen’s list of debts.

entities.name: Wren
entities.body: The auctioneer at whose sale there was an old crock of a safety bicycle the other day, but a lady’s — in Bloom’s plan for cycling down the canal to see Milly. The modern edition drops the sentence.

entities.name: Fogarty
entities.body: Our friend Fogarty, whom Mr Power wonders about and Mr Dedalus says to ask Tom Kernan about: though lost to sight, to memory dear — which means Kernan owes him money.

entities.name: Jimmy Geary
entities.body: The sexton, before whose door an old tramp sat emptying the dirt and stones out of his boot. After life’s journey.

entities.name: Childs
entities.body: Murdered in the last house of the gloomy gardens. His brother was tried for it and Seymour Bushe got him off; the crown had no evidence, only circumstantial. A later episode gives the name: Samuel Childs.

entities.name: Seymour Bushe
entities.body: The K.C. who got him off, and whose polished periods the newspaper men remember in episode 7.

entities.name: Mrs Riordan
entities.body: Who died in Our Lady’s Hospice for the dying: her feeding cup, and the screen round her bed for her to die. Molly knew her at the City Arms hotel.

entities.name: Mesias
entities.body: The tailor who is to turn Bloom’s grey suit. One in a million, Bloom calls him later. Episode 11 gives him his full style: George Robert Mesias, tailor and cutter, of number five Eden quay, who made the indigoblue serge suit of the young gentleman in the hackney car.

entities.name: Alderman Hooper
entities.body: Who gave the Blooms a stuffed bird as a wedding present. Not the Paddy Hooper of the newspaper office.

entities.name: Robert Emery
entities.body: Whose remains are laid in the crypt where the rat goes in — and whose name sets Bloom thinking of the other Robert, buried here by torchlight.

entities.name: Robert Emmet
entities.body: Who was buried here by torchlight, wasn’t he? His last words come back to Bloom in episode 11, in a shop window with seven last words.

entities.name: Mrs Sinico
entities.body: At whose funeral Bloom was last in this cemetery. Emily Sinico, accidentally killed at Sydney Parade railway station.

entities.name: Bloom’s mother
entities.body: Mamma, poor mamma, buried in the plot he bought towards Finglas, with little Rudy. She is not named in this episode.

entities.name: Albert
entities.body: The prince consort, with Victoria on the guncarriage and at the Frogmore memorial: consort not even a king, in Bloom’s account of the old queen’s widowhood. Her son was the substance.

entities.name: Lazarus
entities.body: Come forth, Lazarus! And he came fifth and lost the job — Bloom’s answer to the resurrection and the life.

entities.name: Robinson Crusoe
entities.body: Say Robinson Crusoe was true to life: then Friday buried him. Only man buries — no, ants too.

entities.name: Friday
entities.body: Who buried him. The second Friday in the sentence is the day of the week, and carries no card.

entities.name: Red Murray
entities.body: Who cuts Keyes’s advertisement out of the paper with his long shears in four clean strokes, offers a par to go with it, and whispers that Brayden’s face is like Our Saviour’s.

entities.name: Davy Stephens
entities.body: Minute in a large capecoat, a small felt hat crowning his ringlets, who passes out of Ruttledge’s office with a roll of papers under his cape: a king’s courier.

entities.name: William Brayden
entities.body: Of Oaklands, Sandymount: the stately figure who goes up the staircase steered by an umbrella, a solemn beardframed face. Simon Dedalus says all his brains are in the nape of his neck.

entities.name: Councillor Nannetti
entities.body: The foreman of the machine room, who takes Bloom’s cutting, scratches under his alpaca jacket, and says we can do that, let him give us a three months’ renewal. Member for College green, and soon to be called my lord mayor. He does not hear the machines.

entities.name: Monks
entities.body: The dayfather: an old man, bowed, spectacled, aproned, called for four times across the caseroom to find the archbishop’s letter. Queer lot of stuff he must have put through his hands in his time.

entities.name: Professor MacHugh
entities.body: Unshaven and blackspectacled, eating water biscuits by the window, who teaches the blatant Latin language and would rather profess Greek. He jeers at Dan Dawson’s speech, sets Rome’s cloacal obsession against the radiance of the intellect, and recites John F Taylor’s speech from memory.

entities.name: J. J. O’Molloy
entities.body: Cleverest fellow at the junior bar he used to be, with a hectic flush and practice dwindling, turning the pink pages of the file and asking the editor for money he does not get. He quotes Seymour Bushe on the Moses of Michelangelo. The others call him Jack.

entities.name: Myles Crawford
entities.body: The editor: a scarlet beaked face crested by a comb of feathery hair, bold blue eyes, in and out of his sanctum all afternoon, jingling his keys, declaiming, and pretty well on. He tells Stephen to write something with a bite in it, and sends Keyes a message that will not go into a newspaper.

entities.name: Lenehan
entities.body: Who comes out of the inner office with Sport’s tissues, gives the Gold cup to Sceptre with O. Madden up, lights everybody’s cigarettes, and will not be put off his riddle: what opera resembles a railwayline? The Rose of Castile. Rows of cast steel. In episode 11 he waits in the Ormond for Boylan with impatience, peeps round the sandwichbell at Miss Kennedy, drones his solfa fable of the fox and the stork at her in vain, and coaxes Miss Douce into sounding her garter: Sonnez la cloche! O do! There’s no-one. Then Boylan walks out on him.

entities.name: Mr O’Madden Burke
entities.body: Tall in copious grey of Donegal tweed, who brings Stephen in — Youth led by Experience visits Notoriety — and speaks in the manner of a man quoting himself. They went forth to battle, but they always fell.

entities.name: The newsboy
entities.body: Seized by the collar as the others scamper down the steps: it wasn’t me, sir, it was the big fellow shoved me, sir. He was waiting for the racing special.

entities.name: Pat Farrell
entities.body: The big fellow who shoved him, named by the boy and pointed out round the doorframe.

entities.name: Alexander Keyes
entities.body: Tea, wine and spirit merchant, whose advertisement Bloom is trying to renew: two crossed keys, a circle, and the house of keys — innuendo of home rule, from the Manx parliament. He gets a two months’ renewal and an answer from the editor that Bloom does not deliver.

entities.name: Ruttledge
entities.body: Whose office door creaks and whispers ee: cree, twice, and again in Bloom’s ear in episode 11.

entities.name: Mario
entities.body: The tenor, who was said to be the picture of Our Saviour: Jesusmario with rougy cheeks, doublet and spindle legs, singing in Martha.

entities.name: Long John
entities.body: Who is backing Nannetti for lord mayor, they say. The modern edition gives him the surname here that the older one keeps until episode 10: Long John Fanning, the subsheriff.

entities.name: Phil Blake
entities.body: Of the weekly Pat and Bull story in the Freeman, in Bloom’s list of what really sells a paper. Not the Blake of Stephen’s thought in episode 2.

entities.name: Hedges Eyre Chatterton
entities.body: The vicechancellor, Ned Lambert’s granduncle or greatgranduncle, close on ninety and living to spite them: he writes an odd shaky cheque or two on gale days. Not the Master Abraham Chatterton of episode 15.

entities.name: Wetherup
entities.body: Who always said that: get a grip of them by the stomach.

entities.name: Gabriel Conroy
entities.body: With whom J. J. O’Molloy is believed to do some literary work for the Express.

entities.name: O. Madden
entities.body: Up on Sceptre, the dead cert for the Gold cup that Lenehan gives out and that does not win.

entities.name: Kendal Bushe
entities.body: Whom the editor names and corrects himself out of: Kendal Bushe or I mean Seymour Bushe. An earlier man of the same family and the same reputation at the bar.

entities.name: Chief baron Palles
entities.body: Of the story J. J. O’Molloy begins at the royal university dinner and never finishes, because Lenehan wants his riddle first.

entities.name: Whiteside
entities.body: A master of forensic eloquence, first of the editor’s three men at the bar, with Isaac Butt and silvertongued O’Hagan. Where have you a man now like those fellows?

entities.name: Isaac Butt
entities.body: The second of them.

entities.name: O’Hagan
entities.body: Silvertongued, the third.

entities.name: Henry Grattan
entities.body: Who wrote for this very paper, with Flood: Irish volunteers, established 1763. J. J. O’Molloy brings him in as an orator and the editor takes him back as a journalist.

entities.name: Flood
entities.body: The other of the two. Not the flood of the year Hamilton Long’s was founded.

entities.name: Demosthenes
entities.body: Named in the same list, with Edmund Burke, as the eloquence J. J. O’Molloy will not be told the bar has lost.

entities.name: Edmund Burke
entities.body: The last of the list. Not the O’Madden Burke in the room.

entities.name: Harmsworth
entities.body: Of the farthing press, Ignatius Gallaher’s Chapelizod boss.

entities.name: Dr Lucas
entities.body: Named with the paper’s founding: established 1763.

entities.name: John Philpot Curran
entities.body: Who have you now like him, the editor asks. Not the Curran of Stephen’s list of debts, nor Sara Curran.

entities.name: Tim Healy
entities.body: Sitting with Gerald Fitzgibbon, rumour has it, on the Trinity college estates commission.

entities.name: Gerald Fitzgibbon
entities.body: Mr Justice Fitzgibbon, the present lord justice of appeal, whose speech to the youth of Ireland John F Taylor rose to answer. You know Gerald Fitzgibbon: then you can imagine the style of his discourse. Not Fitzgibbon street.

entities.name: John F Taylor
entities.body: Who had come from a sickbed, with a growth of shaggy beard and a loose white silk neckcloth, and made the finest display of oratory professor MacHugh ever heard — the speech of the Egyptian highpriest to the youthful Moses, which MacHugh gives back from memory in the office.

entities.name: Professor Magennis
entities.body: Who was speaking to J. J. O’Molloy about Stephen, and thinks he must have been pulling A. E.’s leg.

entities.name: Madame Blavatsky
entities.body: That Blavatsky woman, who started the whole thing. A nice old bag of tricks.

entities.name: Skin-the-Goat
entities.body: Fitzharris, who drove the car for an alibi on the day of the Phoenix park murders, and who keeps the cabman’s shelter down at Butt bridge now — they say. Holohan told Mr O’Madden Burke so.

entities.name: Joe Brady
entities.body: One of the invincibles, on the editor’s map of the route and on the commemoration postcard Lady Dudley nearly bought.

entities.name: Tim Kelly
entities.body: Another, whom the editor names and then corrects to Kavanagh.

entities.name: Kavanagh
entities.body: The name he corrects it to. Not Charley Kavanagh of episode 8, nor Kavanagh’s public house.

entities.name: Number One
entities.body: The unnamed head of the invincibles, on the same postcard. The book never gives him another name.

entities.name: Gumley
entities.body: A friend of Stephen’s father, now minding stones for the corporation as a night watchman — let Gumley mind the stones, see they don’t run away.

entities.name: Dick Adams
entities.body: The besthearted bloody Corkman the Lord ever put the breath of life in, present with the editor when Ignatius Gallaher cabled the route to New York.

entities.name: Gregor Grey
entities.body: Who made the design for the advertisement the map was built out of. That gave him the leg up. Not sir John Gray of the statue.

entities.name: Paddy Hooper
entities.body: Who worked Tay Pay and got Gallaher his opening, and who is round at the Oval now with Jack Hall. Not the alderman Hooper of the stuffed owl.

entities.name: Jack Hall
entities.body: With whom he came over last night.

entities.name: Tay Pay
entities.body: T. P. O’Connor, who took Gallaher on to the Star. The older edition spells him as the initials are said; the modern edition writes the name.

entities.name: Blumenfeld
entities.body: Whom Gallaher is in with now.

entities.name: Pyatt
entities.body: He was all their daddies, the editor says. Lenehan makes him the father of scare journalism and the brother-in-law of Chris Callinan.

entities.name: Chris Callinan
entities.body: His brother-in-law, in Lenehan’s footnote. Lenehan tells a longer story about him and Bloom on the Featherbed Mountain in episode 10.

entities.name: Lady Dudley
entities.body: Walking home through the park to see the trees blown down by the cyclone, who thought she would buy a view of Dublin and was offered a commemoration postcard of Joe Brady instead. Right outside the viceregal lodge, imagine.

entities.name: General Bobrikoff
entities.body: The lord lieutenant of Finland, shot. You look as though you had done the deed, J. J. O’Molloy tells Stephen and Mr O’Madden Burke, looking at their ties.

entities.name: Jakes M’Carthy
entities.body: Father, Son and Holy Ghost and Jakes M’Carthy — the editor’s formula for putting everybody into it. The modern edition spells him McCarthy.

entities.name: Xenophon
entities.body: Who looked upon Marathon, and Marathon looked on the sea: Mr Dedalus quoting Byron at Dan Dawson’s prose.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: A recently discovered fragment of whom, professor MacHugh says with pomp of tone, is Dan Dawson’s speech in this morning’s paper.

entities.name: Sallust
entities.body: In mourning for whom, Mulligan says of professor MacHugh’s black clothes. Whose mother is beastly dead.

entities.name: Lord Salisbury
entities.body: A sofa in a westend club — where professor MacHugh looks for the spirituality of the Roman and the Englishman and does not find it.

entities.name: Maximilian Karl O’Donnell
entities.body: Graf von Tirconnell in Ireland, the Irishman who saved the emperor’s life on the ramparts of Vienna and whose heir was sent over to make the king an Austrian fieldmarshal. Wild geese.

entities.name: Macduff
entities.body: Lay on, Macduff — Mr O’Madden Burke’s word for going to Mooney’s, with a lunge of his umbrella.

entities.name: Michelangelo
entities.body: Whose Moses in the vatican Seymour Bushe cited, and described in the period J. J. O’Molloy repeats: that stony effigy in frozen music, horned and terrible. Not the Michelangelo Hayes of episode 12.

entities.name: Moses
entities.body: Twice over in this episode: the statue in the vatican, and the youthful Moses of John F Taylor’s speech, who did not listen to the Egyptian highpriest and so brought the chosen people out of their house of bondage. He died without having entered the land of promise, which is where Stephen’s parable of the plums ends up.

entities.name: Saint Augustine
